title: Structural changes
sub: Why adding a component costs more than writing one, what a sync point is, and how an EntityCommandBuffer gets you around it
cards/0/title: A structural change moves the entity to another chunk
cards/0/body:
A structural change is anything that changes an entity’s archetype or the set of chunks: creating or destroying an entity, adding or removing a component, changing the value of a shared component (ISharedComponentData: its value is one per chunk, so a new value means a different chunk).

The mechanism: the entity gets a new archetype, so all of its components are copied into a chunk of that archetype, and the hole in the old chunk is filled by the last entity. That is memory copying plus bookkeeping, not a single field write.

Writing a value of a regular component — SetComponentData, or a write through RefRW in a job — is not a structural change: the entity stays where it is. One more consequence: after a structural change, direct references to component data (a DynamicBuffer, for example) become invalid.
cards/1/title: Sync point: the main thread waits for every job
cards/1/body:
Structural changes through EntityManager run on the main thread only, and before rearranging chunks Entities waits for every job scheduled so far — any of them might be reading those chunks. That spot is called a sync point.

The cost is not the operation itself but what it does to the frame. You scheduled movement and damage as jobs, the workers have just started — and an AddComponent in the middle of OnUpdate makes the main thread stand still until they finish. The parallelism Entities built between systems is cut off.

Run() on a job and a main-thread foreach over a query also create sync points if a job is still writing the data. In the Profiler it shows up as a main-thread wait in the middle of the systems.
cards/1/flow/2: the main thread waits for every job
cards/2/q: Which of these are structural changes? Select all that apply.
cards/2/explain: Adding a component and creating an entity change the archetype or add an entity. A shared component’s value is one per chunk, so changing it moves the entity to another chunk. Writing a regular component’s value leaves the entity in place — it is just a memory write.
cards/3/q: Which line creates a sync point in the middle of the frame?
cards/3/explain: Instantiate creates an entity — a structural change. The main thread waits for MoveJob and PoisonJob and only then schedules AimJob. Spawning the bullet should be deferred and done in one batch at the end of the system group — the next card shows how.
cards/4/body:
An EntityCommandBuffer (ECB) is a list of deferred commands: “create”, “destroy”, “add a component”. You can record them from the main thread or from a job; Playback applies them — always on the main thread, as one batch.

Usually you take a buffer from a playback system: EndSimulationEntityCommandBufferSystem plays its buffers back at the end of the simulation group. GetSingleton registers your job with that system, so it waits for the job before playing back. You never call Playback or Dispose on such a buffer yourself — that is its job. This way the structural changes of many systems land in one spot instead of tearing the frame in ten places.

From a parallel job you record through ecb.AsParallelWriter() — an EntityCommandBuffer.ParallelWriter. Each of its commands takes a sort key as the first argument: threads record in a jumbled order, and before playback the commands are sorted by key. The key must not depend on how the job was spread over threads; the standard one is a [ChunkIndexInQuery] int parameter of Execute.

And a rule: no structural changes through EntityManager inside a foreach over SystemAPI.Query — the iteration walks chunks that the change would rearrange, and in the Editor you get an InvalidOperationException, “Structural changes are not allowed during iteration”. The way out is to record the commands into an ECB inside the loop and play it back after the loop. And if you change everything a query matches, there are batch calls over the whole query, such as EntityManager.DestroyEntity(query) with an EntityQuery object.
cards/5/q: Why does ParallelWriter take a sortKey as the first argument of every command?
cards/5/options/0: So the playback order does not depend on how work was spread over threads: commands are sorted by key before Playback
cards/5/options/1: It is the worker thread index, used to pick that thread’s part of the buffer
cards/5/options/2: Without it DestroyEntity cannot find the entity
cards/5/options/3: The key sets the frame in which the command runs
cards/5/explain: Threads record commands in an unpredictable order. A key tied to the chunk in the query (ChunkIndexInQuery) does not depend on scheduling, so after sorting the playback is deterministic.
cards/5/wrong/1: The key sets order, not a thread. Using the thread index would make the order depend on scheduling — the very thing to avoid.
cards/5/wrong/2: The entity is passed as a separate argument; the key has nothing to do with finding it.
cards/5/wrong/3: When to play back is decided by the system that owns the buffer, not by the key.
cards/6/title: Your own buffer, and its price
cards/6/body:
You can create a buffer yourself: new EntityCommandBuffer(Allocator.TempJob). Then everything is on you: wait for the job, call Playback(state.EntityManager) and Dispose().

Remember: an ECB does not make structural changes free. Playback is the same structural changes on the main thread. An ECB wins by moving them — from the middle of the frame to a point where jobs are finished anyway — and by batching them instead of scattered calls.

Your own buffer is justified when you need the result right now, in the same system. Otherwise take one from an ECB system.
cards/7/task: Rewrite DeathSystem: destroying dead entities (Health.Value <= 0) must be recorded into an ECB from a parallel job, not done through EntityManager inside the iteration. In DestroyDeadJob add an EntityCommandBuffer.ParallelWriter field, a [ChunkIndexInQuery] int sort key and a DestroyEntity(key, entity) call. In OnUpdate get the buffer from EndSimulationEntityCommandBufferSystem with CreateCommandBuffer(state.WorldUnmanaged) and pass it to the job through AsParallelWriter().
cards/7/checks/1/label: Execute receives a sort key via [ChunkIndexInQuery] int
cards/7/checks/2/label: The destruction is recorded: DestroyEntity(key, entity)
cards/7/checks/3/label: The buffer comes from EndSimulationEntityCommandBufferSystem via CreateCommandBuffer(state.WorldUnmanaged) and goes to the job via AsParallelWriter()
cards/7/checks/5/label: No manual Playback() or Dispose(): the ECB system does them
cards/7/explain: The job only records commands, and the workers never wait for the main thread. EndSimulationEntityCommandBufferSystem waits for the job itself, sorts the commands by ChunkIndexInQuery and plays them back as one batch at the end of the simulation group, where the jobs are finished anyway. In the interview: “structural changes are sync points, so I record them into an ECB from the job and play them back in one spot”.
cards/8/q: Put in order what happens to ECB commands during a frame.
cards/8/items/0: A system takes a buffer from EndSimulationEntityCommandBufferSystem
cards/8/items/1: A job on the workers records commands through ParallelWriter
cards/8/items/2: The other systems of the simulation group run; chunks do not change
cards/8/items/3: The ECB system waits for the jobs that wrote to the buffer
cards/8/items/4: Commands are sorted by key and played back on the main thread
cards/8/items/5: The ECB system disposes the buffer
cards/8/explain: While commands are only recorded, the chunk layout does not change, and all systems run in parallel. The structural changes happen once — at playback, at the end of the group.
cards/9/title: Enableable components: toggle without a structural change
cards/9/body:
If a state switches on and off often — stunned, in combat, seen by the camera — adding and removing a component is expensive. That is what IEnableableComponent is for: the component stays in the archetype, and each entity has an “enabled” bit.

SetComponentEnabled<T>(entity, bool) flips only that bit: the archetype stays the same, the entity does not move, and there is no structural change and no full sync point. But the call through EntityManager, like SetComponentData, first waits for the jobs that read or write T. So in hot code you toggle from worker threads, through ComponentLookup<T>.SetComponentEnabled — the job needs write access to T.

Queries treat a disabled component as missing: an entity with Stunned disabled does not match a query that needs Stunned. You can still read and modify a disabled component’s data.

The price: disabled components still sit in the chunks, and jobs over those archetypes check the bits and may run slower. For rare changes the docs recommend plain adding and removing.
cards/10/q: A unit gains the “Rage” ability once per match and keeps it until the end. Make it an enableable component, or add a component?
cards/10/options/0: Add the component through an ECB: the change is rare, and a disabled component would sit in the chunk all match long and slow down jobs over that archetype
cards/10/options/1: Enableable: flipping a bit is always cheaper, so structural changes should be avoided everywhere
cards/10/options/2: Keep a bool in another component and check it with an if in every job
cards/10/explain: Enableable pays off when there are many toggles. One change per match through an ECB costs next to nothing, while a permanently disabled component is extra bytes in the chunk and a bit check on every pass.
cards/10/wrong/1: A structural change is expensive when it is frequent or mid-frame. One deferred into an ECB is cheap.
cards/10/wrong/2: That is the same check, done by hand and without the queries’ help: every job would walk the units without Rage too.
cards/10/wrong/3: EntityManager is not available in a job: structural changes happen on the main thread only; from a job, go through an ECB.
cards/11/q: Match each situation with the tool
cards/11/pairs/0/0: A stun turns on and off many times a second
cards/11/pairs/1/0: Destroy an entity from a parallel job
cards/11/pairs/2/1: write the component: not a structural change
cards/11/pairs/3/0: The commands’ result is needed right now, in the same system
cards/11/pairs/3/1: your own ECB: Complete, Playback, Dispose
